native_result.query: What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?
native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.
native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality increased substantially for both white males and white females in the NLSY79 cohort. The shifted Gini coefficient rose from 0.255 to 0.464 (males) and from 0.080 to 0.429 (females), and the P90/P50 ratio more than doubled in both groups. The increase was larger in absolute terms for females (+0.349 vs +0.208), but this reflected a much lower 1990 baseline. The initial inter-sex inequality gap (Gini gap +0.18 in 1990, males more unequal) essentially closed by 1996 (gap +0.03), with both groups converging to nearly identical inequality levels. The polarisation was driven by: (1) the zero-wealth share nearly doubling (males 25.7%→43.3%, females 20.3%→42.6%), (2) the median falling sharply (males $15.6k→$8.9k, females $20.1k→$8.8k), and (3) the mean rising (males $88k→$132k, females $100k→$129k), indicating wealth gains concentrated at the top.
native_result.WorkflowB: Filtered race=='white' (n=7,099), split by sex (male n=3,469; female n=3,630). Computed Gini (shifted for negative values), P90/P50 ratio, CV, mean-median gap, and variance for composite_wealth_1990 and composite_wealth_1996 in each subgroup. Compared intra-sex (1990→1996) and inter-sex (male vs female) changes. No sampling weights applied (weight=1 per observation).

native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: Individuals with a criminal record (ever_jailed=1) had significantly lower wealth than those without a criminal record in all three measured years: 1985, 1990, and 1996. Mann-Whitney U one-sided tests (alpha=0.05) gave p=8.0e-11 (1985), p=3.9e-35 (1990), and p=4.6e-26 (1996), all far below the significance threshold and below a Bonferroni-corrected threshold (alpha=0.0167); Welch t-tests and a permutation test on mean differences confirmed the result in every year.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; validated 0 nulls). Split into groups by ever_jailed (jailed N=289 vs. no-jailed N=11,724). For each year (1985, 1990, 1996), compared composite wealth between groups with a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test (alpha=0.05) and reported two-sided p-values. Ran sensitivity checks: Welch t-test and a 20,000-permutation test on the mean difference. Applied a Bonferroni multiple-comparison check (alpha=0.05/3). Conclusion: significantly lower wealth for the jailed group in all three years.

Fit nested OLS with listwise deletion: Model R = SES block (log family income 1979, mother's grade, father's grade) + race dummies (Black, Hispanic; ref non-Black/non-Hispanic) + demographics (sex, age 1979, family size); Model F = Model R + ASVAB composite. Compared SES/race coefficients and R2 between models and ran a nested F-test for the academic block. Sensitivities: (a) four individual ASVAB scores, (b) added class-rank percentile (complete case), (c) added family net wealth 1985, (d) multiple imputation m=20 on income and parental grades; also attempted an ordered-logit secondary (did not converge). native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 data, socioeconomic status is the primary driver of the racial difference in BA-track educational progress. As of 1979 (ages 14-22), Black students show no overall advantage: 3.6% had completed >=14 grades (2+ years of college) vs 7.4% of non-Black/non-Hispanic students. The Black-non-Black gap is concentrated at low family income (2.7% vs 12.0%; adjusted OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17-0.53), shrinks at mid income (3.4% vs 4.7%; OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.72-1.98, n.s.) and disappears at high income (6.3% vs 6.7%; OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.57-1.55, n.s.); the Hispanic pattern is identical (Low OR 0.44, Mid 0.94, High 1.21, the latter two n.s.). The race x SES interaction is statistically significant (Black x Mid OR 3.95 [1.86, 8.40]; Black x High OR 3.11 [1.47, 6.60]). Thus, the observed racial gap in BA-track progress is a low-SES phenomenon: at mid and high family income levels, Black and non-Black students reach college progress at statistically indistinguishable rates, so SES level — not race — accounts for the divergence.

IMPORTANT: there is NO real BA-completion variable and no post-1979 education waves; the outcome is a proxy — educational progress as of 1979 when respondents were 14-22 years old ('Highest grade completed, 1979' >= 14 = 2+ years of college; code 95 treated as missing). 2) SES constructed (no pre-categorized SES exists): terciles of log1p(total net family income, previous calendar year 1978, recorded 1979) — the most complete pre-outcome measure (80.4% non-missing); income top-coded at 75,001 retained. 3) ASVAB composite (mean of 4 sections) was NOT a real z-score (raw mean ~476, SD ~91) so we standardized it ourselves, z=(x-mean)/sd; because it was measured in 1981 (after the 1979 outcome) it was excluded from primary models and used only as an exploratory sensitivity control. 4) Descriptive cross-tabs of the outcome by race x SES tertile with Wilson 95% CIs. 5) Logistic regressions: M1 race only, M2 +SES, M3 +SES+age+sex+family size (primary), M4 race x SES interaction with cell-specific ORs (vs same-SES non-Black/non-Hispanic reference) with Wald-based 95% CIs. 6) Sensitivity: outcomes >=13 and >=16; SES from 1985 income and 1985 wealth; ASVAB-adjusted model. Analysis sample n=10,071 (listwise: grade + 1979 income available); income missingness is mildly differential by race (Black 17.4% vs Non-Black 20.1%).

native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: From 1985 through 1996, the median family net wealth of non-Black, non-Hispanic (predominantly white) respondents was consistently and substantially higher than that of both Black and Hispanic respondents, and the racial wealth gap widened over time. In 1985, the median wealth of the non-Black, non-Hispanic group was $3,500, compared to $1,600 for Black respondents (2.2×) and $500 for Hispanic respondents (7.0×). By 1990, the gap had widened to $12,972 vs. $4,800 (2.7×) and $1,600 (8.1×). By 1996, the median for the non-Black, non-Hispanic group reached $42,600, compared to $9,800 for Black respondents (4.3×) and $2,562 for Hispanic respondents (16.6×). The Hispanic median remained the lowest in all three years; the Black-to-Hispanic ratio fluctuated (3.2× in 1985, 3.0× in 1990, 3.8× in 1996) but did not close. These findings are based on the NLSY79 panel (n = 12,686), treating the 'NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC' category (code 3) as a proxy for white respondents. Wealth missingness increased over the panel (20% in 1985 to 45% in 1996) and was differential by race (52.6% for the non-Black, non-Hispanic group in 1996), so the 1996 medians reflect a smaller, potentially non-representative subsample. A sensitivity check on the 1985∩1996 subsample confirmed that the direction and magnitude of the gaps are robust to attrition.

By 1990, the gap had widened to $12,972 vs. $4,800 (2.7×) and $1,600 (8.1×). By 1996, the median for the non-Black, non-Hispanic group reached $42,600, compared to $9,800 for Black respondents (4.3×) and $2,562 for Hispanic respondents (16.6×). The Hispanic median remained the lowest in all three years; the Black-to-Hispanic ratio fluctuated (3.2× in 1985, 3.0× in 1990, 3.8× in 1996) but did not close. native_result.query: Is the relation between socioeconomic status and chances of degree completion affected by racial lines of the individual?
native_result.HypoA: The strength and significance of the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and BA degree completion differ across racial groups. For Whites, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.2169 (p = 0.031). For Blacks SES has a larger positive coefficient of 0.9775 (p < 0.001). For Hispanics, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.6724 (p = 0.013).
native_result.HypoB: Yes — the SES -> bachelor's-degree-completion relationship is modulated by race. The positive SES slope is significantly steeper for Black respondents (and directionally for Hispanic respondents) than for White respondents. In a logistic model of BA completion on SES (continuous, per +1 SD) x race (reference = White), each +1 SD of SES multiplies the odds of degree completion by ~1.18 in Whites (p=.031), ~1.65 in Hispanics (p=.013) and ~2.07 in Blacks (p<.001); the Black x SES interaction OR is 1.76 (95% CI 1.21-2.55, p=.003) and the joint SES x race interaction test is significant (likelihood-ratio p=.008; Wald p=.006), i.e., there is statistically significant racial heterogeneity of the SES effect. The moderation is robust to adjusting for cognitive ability (direct-effect model with ASVAB + class percentile: Black x SES OR 1.75, p=.006) but is partly explained by family size (joint interaction p=.28 after adding sex + family size). Whites nonetheless have higher completion at every SES level (base rate ~3.5% vs ~1.3-1.4% for Black/Hispanic), so the benefit of higher SES is concentrated in the Black and Hispanic groups even though their absolute completion remains lower. Caveats: BA completion is rare (236/8773 = 2.7%) and Black/Hispanic strata have only 19-28 events, so interaction estimates have wide CIs and limited power; the Hispanic x SES term is not individually significant.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (N=8773, 0 missing), dropped the spurious row-index column, standardized SES/ASVAB/percentile to z-scores, and one-hot encoded SAMPLE_RACE with reference = White. M1 (total effect): logistic BA ~ SES_z * RACE, no ability covariates; homogeneity of effect tested with a likelihood-ratio test (full vs main-effects, df=2) plus a joint Wald test of the two SES x race interaction terms (continuous-exposure analogue of Breslow-Day). Stratification: per-race logistic SES slope with 95% CI, a crosstab of BA rate by race x SES tercile reporting events/n, and predicted-probability curves vs SES by race (exported to artifacts/pred_prob_curves_M1.csv since matplotlib was unavailable). M2 added SAMPLE_SEX and FAMILY SIZE; M3 added ASVAB_z and PERCENTILE_z as a direct-effect/sensitivity analysis. Firth bias-reduced logistic (implemented manually, no external package) was run as a cross-check; standard MLE converged for all models so it was reported as primary. native_result.HypoB: The Black students' advantage in BA-completion rates relative to White peers is most pronounced at the highest SES levels (top SES tercile, and within it the top decile, SES ≳ 0.95): there the Black−White gap is at its minimum and inverts (Black 6.1% vs White 4.9%), the adjusted Black×SES interaction is positive (Black odds ~1.37× per +1 SES; ~3.1× in the high-tercile), and SES lifts Black completion ~5× (Low→High) vs ~1.25× for White.
native_result.WorkflowB: Inspection (8773x8, 0 missing, SES continuous [-2.45,2.72], BA-completed base rate 2.69%) -> descriptive completion tables by race x SES tertile & decile with Wilson 95% CIs, Black-White abs gap and Black/White ratio -> logistic regression BA ~ race(Black)+race(Hispanic) + SES + Black*SES + ABILITY + SAMPLE_SEX + FAMILY SIZE, reporting the Black x SES interaction coef with 95% CI, plus a binned-SES logit for robustness and a Black-vs-own-low-SES-baseline relative-boost check -> interpretation: positive differential slope means the Black-White gap shrinks as SES rises, so the advantage is most pronounced at high SES (top tercile / top decile).

native_result.query: Between which two races is the factor of BA degree completion -0.9568 when compared to the other?
native_result.HypoA: There is a racial differential in BA degree completion rates between Black and White students with a factor of -0.9568.
native_result.HypoB: The -0.9568 factor is the log-odds (logit) coefficient of a univariate logistic regression of BA degree completion on race with White as the reference category, and it corresponds to the Hispanic vs. White comparison: Hispanic respondents have log-odds of BA completion 0.9568 lower than White respondents', an odds ratio of exp(-0.9568) ≈ 0.384, i.e. about 62% lower odds of completing a BA than White respondents.
native_result.WorkflowB: Executed and reproducible via analysis_ba_race.py (output in analysis_output.txt). native_result.query: Which technique is considered the most commonly used by respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 69.399% indicating so (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: Interviews (69.399% respondents saying so, 95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) are the most commonly used technique considered by the respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: Interviews is the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: 50.0% of the 194 valid respondents (97/194) indicated using interviews, the highest share among the six Q9 techniques (Scenarios 38.66%, Prototyping 38.66%, Workshops/Meetings 38.14%, Observation 32.99%, Others 5.67%), with a respondent-level bootstrap 95% CI of [42.78%, 57.22%] (B=10,000, seed=42).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/requirements_engineering_for_ML-enabled_systems.csv (276 respondents x 202 columns). 2) Mapped the no-answer block code '-77' to NaN on the six Q9_ML_Elicitation_* variables and restricted the analysis to the 194 respondents with complete Q9 (the 82 excluded rows are exactly the 'Suspended (22)' respondents who skipped the block; '-99'/'-66' appear only in free-text fields). 3) Computed per-technique usage as the proportion of 'quoted' (used) among the 194 valid respondents. 4) Selected the most common technique by argmax of the proportions: Interviews (97/194 = 50.000%). 5) Ran a nonparametric respondent-level bootstrap (resampling the 194 rows with replacement, B=10,000, numpy default_rng seed=42), recomputing the 'quoted' proportion per technique in each resample, and took the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles as the 95% CI: Interviews [42.784, 57.216]; Scenarios [31.959, 45.361]; Prototyping [31.959, 45.361]; Workshops/Meetings [31.443, 44.845]; Observation [26.289, 39.691]; Others [2.577, 9.278]. 6) Sensitivity: with denominator 276 (suspended counted as not used) Interviews remains rank 1 (35.145%); the ranking is identical to the n=194 case. 7) Reproducibility note: the question's stated 69.399% [69.062, 69.735] is not reproducible from this binarized CSV under any tested proportion definition (max 50.0% at n=194; 127/183=69.3989% matches the point estimate but no Q9 column has that count, and the stated +/-0.34 pp CI is far narrower than a respondent-level bootstrap at n~194), so the data-grounded figure reported is 50.0% on 194 valid respondents.

native_result.query: How does age influence the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in?
native_result.HypoA: Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they had put in and with a negative coefficient between age and withdrawing more than putting into savings (-0.0422).
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. One-hot encode Gender variable into MALE and FEMALE
2. Extract the independent variables ['AGE','INCOME', 'BMI', 'BLACK', 'HISPANIC', 'MALE', 'FEMALE']
3. Add dependent variable (DISSAVED) from the df
4. Add a constant term to the independent variable to account for the intercept term in the logistic regression model.
5. Fit a logistic regression model
native_result.HypoB: Among young NLSY79 respondents in the 1989 cross-section (ages 24-32), being older is modestly negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more from savings than putting in (DISSAVED=1). In a headline logistic model controlling for income, gender, BMI and race, each additional year of age is associated with ~4.7% lower odds of DISSAVED=1 (OR ~0.95, 95% CI 0.935-0.970) and ~1 percentage point lower probability (average marginal effect ~-0.96 pp/yr; predicted probability falls from ~25% at age 24 to ~18% at age 32). The relationship is weakly non-linear (shallow mid-20s peak then steeper decline into the early 30s; quadratic term p~0.046) and the overall association is small (pseudo R^2 ~0.006), so it is a modest, associative pattern confined to the 24-32 window. Under a time-preference reading, net dissaving proxies higher discounting/lower patience, so the gradient is consistent with older youth being slightly more patient savers, though the effect is too small to be economically large.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686 rows, 0 missing). Constructed centered age AGE_c and AGE2_c (resolves raw AGE/AGE_2 collinearity, VIF 686->~1), log1p(INCOME), MALE dummy, winsorized BMI. Fitted (a) headline logistic DISSAVED ~ AGE_c+AGE2_c+LOGINC+BMI+MALE+BLACK+HISPANIC, (b) no-income sensitivity, (c) BMI-winsorized sensitivity. Computed average marginal effect of +1 yr age, predicted P at ages 24/28/32 at mean covariates, per-age observed rates, quadratic-vs-linear Wald test, and supplementary P(DISSAVED=1|SAMESAVE=0). Association only (1989 cross-section).

Predicted probability at mean covariates declines from approximately 25% at age 24 to 18% at age 32. The overall association is small (pseudo R² approximately 0.006).

native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Un mayor time preference (preferencia por el presente, proxy=menor comportamiento de ahorro en 1989) se asocia con un BMI modestamente mayor, pero la asociación es débil y correlacional: ~0.21 unidades de BMI por paso hacia menos paciencia (~0.64 en el rango completo), estadísticamente significativo pero pequeño en magnitud, no causal.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Carga y validación de nls_raw.csv (12,686 obs). 2) Detección de problemas de calidad: peso en libras (no kg) y estatura 1981 corrupta -> uso estatura 1985. 3) BMI = 703*peso1989(lb)/estatura1985(in)^2, trim 12-60. 4) Proxy ordinal de time preference por categoria de ahorro 1989 (1 mas paciente -> 4 menos paciente). 5) Medias por categoria. 6) OLS BMI ~ tp_score + covariables (sexo, raza, edad, tam familiar, ingreso, residencia). 7) Robustez: version binaria y modelo crudo. 8) Sensibilidad: imputacion multiple m=10. 9) Documentacion de sesgo de seleccion por faltantes crecientes de peso.

P0||G0.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?

P0||G0.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
